7.q: A senior manager values keeping staff within their departments to support long-term development, but a project manager worries this limits how much attention projects receive. Which structure often improves staff continuity and career development but may reduce project focus?
7.w: Functional structures keep staff within departments, supporting career development but reducing project focus.

n.0: Project-based structures remove staff from departmental paths.
n.2: Strong matrix prioritises projects more heavily.
n.3: Hybrid can balance both staff development and project focus.
n.1: Agile squads focus fully on delivery.

7.q: A project is being implemented in a school during term time. Which is the most likely dependency to impact the schedule?
o: Design of the signage used around the site
The number of teachers attending progress meetings
School holidays and exam periods restricting project work
Choice of contractor for the classroom refurbishment
Availability of the preferred project management software
7.w: School events often require project work to be scheduled at less disruptive times.

n.3: Documentation style does not create dependencies with BAU.
n.4: Meeting frequency is an internal project factor.
n.1: Presentation format does not create a dependency.
n.0: Supplier choice is a procurement, not a scheduling dependency.

7.q: A risk owner accepts responsibility for several risks but never nominates anyone to carry out the agreed response activities. As delivery continues, what is the most likely outcome of this omission?
o: Increased stakeholder confidence in risk handling
Improved accountability across the whole risk process
Faster resolution of the identified risks
A reduced need for ongoing risk monitoring
Lack of clear responsibility for implementing responses
7.w: Without action owners, responses may not be executed effectively.

n.1: Accountability decreases.
n.2: Resolution may be delayed.
n.3: Monitoring is still required.
n.0: Confidence may drop.

7.q: An organisation is clarifying which responsibilities belong to the project board and which belong to the delivery team, in order to avoid overlap and confusion during delivery. Which TWO responsibilities would normally sit with a project governance body rather than the delivery team?
o: Approving continued investment at key decision points
Resolving every operational issue during delivery
Assigning daily tasks to individual team members
Providing oversight of alignment with organisational objectives
7.w: Governance bodies approve investment decisions and oversee strategic alignment.

n.2: Daily task assignment belongs to delivery management.
n.3: Technical instructions are not normally a governance responsibility.
n.1: Operational issues should usually be managed by the project team unless escalation is needed.

7.q: As part of preparing for a supplier negotiation, the buyer's negotiator sets the least favourable terms at which they would still be willing to close a deal. The negotiator prepares their ______, detailing the worst acceptable outcome.
7.w: The reservation price is the least favorable point at which a negotiator will accept a deal.

n.3: Aspiration price is the ideal target.
n.1: Target price represents the desired outcome.
n.4: ZOPA is the agreement range.
n.2: BATNA is the fallback alternative, not the minimum price.

7.q: A team is documenting the sustainability responsibilities it will carry throughout the planning phase of a public-sector project. Reviewing the draft entries, which of the following is NOT a genuine sustainability responsibility in project planning?
7.w: Overlooking regulations contradicts the responsibility to comply with environmental standards.

n.3: Assessing social impacts is a key sustainability responsibility.
n.4: Resource management ensures efficient consumption.
n.2: Long-term planning is core to sustainable outcomes.
n.1: Supplier monitoring ensures ethical and sustainable sourcing.

7.q: A stakeholder tells the project manager they expect the deliverables sooner than the timescale that was agreed and baselined in the schedule. What should the project manager do in response?
7.w: Reconfirming agreed timelines helps align expectations.

n.4: Acceleration may not be feasible.
n.3: Escalation is not necessary.
n.1: Ignoring worsens misalignment.
n.2: Reducing communication is ineffective.

7.q: During an audit of the team's inclusion practices, a project manager reviews a list of attributes and must identify which one falls outside the scope of equality legislation. Which is NOT a characteristic protected by diversity and inclusion legislation?
7.w: Management style is not protected by equality law.

n.0: Religion or belief is protected by law.
n.3: Pregnancy and maternity are protected.
n.1: Sexual orientation is protected.
n.4: Disability is a protected characteristic.

7.q: During the transition of a new system, a readiness assessment reveals that the receiving support team does not fully understand how to operate it. The project manager wants to close this knowledge gap using practical, complementary measures. Which two actions together would best address a knowledge gap identified during transition?
o: Conducting performance appraisals and salary reviews
Issuing press releases and updating brand guidelines
Creating quick reference guides and hosting Q&A workshops
Ordering new hardware and software licenses
Scheduling daily standups and weekend retreats
7.w: Quick reference guides paired with Q&A workshops build practical knowledge and address questions in real time.

n.1: Press releases focus on public messaging, not internal knowledge transfer.
n.4: Standups and retreats do not target specific knowledge gaps.
n.0: Appraisals and salaries are unrelated to operational know-how.
n.3: Hardware orders do not fill procedural knowledge gaps.

7.q: A trainee project professional is trying to understand how accountability is divided between the two most senior project roles on their assignment. What distinguishes the project sponsor from the project manager in terms of responsibility?
o: The sponsor manages sprint backlog items; the manager funds the project
The sponsor owns the business case; the manager delivers it
The sponsor writes technical specifications; the manager reviews the strategy
The sponsor monitors timesheets; the manager approves the business case
The sponsor plans daily work schedules; the manager sets objectives
7.w: The sponsor ensures continued business justification, while the PM leads delivery.

n.3: Timesheet tracking is an operational task for the PM or support staff.
n.2: Technical documents are produced by technical teams or the PM.
n.4: Work scheduling is managed by the PM.
n.0: Sprint backlog items are managed by product teams.

7.q: A financial services firm is launching a new mobile banking feature. In benefits management, at what stage should the expected return on investment be quantified?
7.w: Quantification of expected ROI is done during definition to set clear benefit parameters.

n.1: Identification identifies potential benefits but doesn't quantify them.
n.4: Planning sets out how to achieve benefits, but quantification happens earlier.
n.2: Tracking monitors benefits, doesn't quantify initial expectations.
n.0: Realisation measures achieved benefits, not initial quantification.

7.q: During execution of a resource-constrained project, two work streams begin competing for the same scarce specialists and their leads cannot agree a way forward. A governance mechanism that helps resolve such conflicts is:
7.w: Escalation procedures provide a formal path to resolve decision conflicts.

n.3: Celebrations don’t address decision conflicts.
n.1: Decor doesn’t influence priority resolution.
n.4: Equipment upgrades aren’t governance tools.
n.2: Snacks are unrelated to governance mechanisms.

7.q: A project manager is preparing a progress report for the sponsor and needs to include a measure that shows how the project is performing against its approved budget. Which factor is most commonly reported to track project budget performance?
7.w: Cost variance shows the difference between budgeted and actual costs, indicating budget performance.

n.3: Schedule variance measures time performance, not budget.
n.4: Open risks count tracks risk exposure, not cost performance.
n.2: Stakeholder satisfaction is a qualitative metric, not a budget measure.
n.1: Defect density relates to quality, not budget.

7.q: A project is technically feasible but conflicts with organisational values, leading to rejection. What aspect of context is most relevant?
7.w: Organisational values are part of internal context.

n.2: Market forces are external.
n.3: Lifecycle is not the issue.
n.0: Mapping is not the core problem.
n.1: Procurement is irrelevant here.

7.q: A sponsor and senior stakeholders want reassurance that the project is being formally scrutinised at defined points before further funding is committed. Which benefit of decision gate reviews most helps stakeholders feel confident in project progress?
o: Ensuring personal recognition for team members
7.w: Structured decision gate checkpoints give stakeholders visibility and confidence in progress.

n.0: Zero errors cannot be guaranteed by reviews alone.
n.4: Reviews mitigate but cannot eliminate all risks.
n.3: Throughput is a productivity metric, not a primary gate benefit.
n.2: Personal recognition is not an inherent deliverable of reviews.

7.q: A team member complains that their line manager and their project manager keep giving them competing instructions about which work to do first. Which organisational structure is most likely to result in conflicting priorities of this kind due to dual reporting lines?
7.w: Matrix structures often lead to conflicting priorities due to shared authority between project and functional managers.

n.4: Project-based structures have a single reporting line to the project manager.
n.1: Functional structures involve clear departmental authority.
n.2: Agile teams are usually self-organising and not subject to multiple reporting lines.
n.0: Product-centric teams have defined ownership, reducing conflict.

7.q: During a project review, two team members read the same status report yet each came away convinced it supported the view they already held about the project's health. Which type of bias does this situation best illustrate?
7.w: Confirmation bias leads recipients to favor information that aligns with existing beliefs.

n.4: Channel bias relates to medium selection, not interpretation preconceptions.
n.3: Temporal bias concerns timing effects, not preconceptions.
n.2: Semantic barriers involve word meanings, not cognitive biases.
n.0: Organizational bias stems from hierarchy, not individual beliefs.

7.q: To strengthen quality assurance across a large programme, a project manager introduces regular process audits for every delivery team. Assuming they are conducted well, what is the MOST likely outcome of this initiative?
7.w: Audits increase confidence in processes.

n.2: Testing is still required.
n.4: Effort may increase.
n.3: Speed is not guaranteed.
n.0: Defects may still occur.

7.q: An organisation is choosing a life cycle for an upcoming initiative and weighing up whether a hybrid approach is warranted by its needs. Which of the following situations would BEST support the selection of a hybrid life cycle?
o: A small team with limited experience
A product requiring regulatory review and fast iteration
A stable, simple project with no changes expected
A project with only one stakeholder
7.w: Hybrid life cycles suit projects that need both compliance with regulation and iterative product development.

n.2: A stable project is more suited to linear.
n.0: Inexperienced teams may struggle with complexity.
n.3: This doesn’t demand a mixed approach.
n.4: Fixed-budget construction typically uses linear models.

7.q: A project manager is planning a project delivered through a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping phases and needs to decide how resources will be committed to the work. Which of the following best describes resource allocation in a linear (waterfall) life cycle?
o: Resources are assigned at random all throughout the whole project
Resource allocation is decided only once the whole project closes
Resources are allocated in advance to each phase, following a sequential plan
Resources can never be adjusted after they are first assigned
All resources are shared across every phase at the same time
7.w: In linear life cycles, resources are assigned to each sequential phase as per the plan.

n.4: Simultaneous resource sharing is more typical of iterative cycles.
n.1: Allocation must occur before closure to deliver the work.
n.3: Resource needs may be reviewed at stage gates.
n.0: Allocation is structured, not random.

7.q: A newly appointed team leader is studying McGregor's Theory X to understand the assumptions it makes about how workers behave and how they should be managed. Which of these is NOT a principle of Theory X?
7.w: Theory X assumes people dislike work and need direction; the idea that employees are self-motivated contradicts Theory X.

n.4: Theory X views work as undesirable and employees as reluctant.
n.3: Theory X holds that workers avoid responsibility.
n.0: Close supervision is characteristic of Theory X managers.
n.1: Under Theory X, people are seen as preferring direction over autonomy.

7.q: A project professional attends a hands-on workshop to learn how to use a new piece of project management software that their organisation is introducing. In terms of continuing professional development, what type of CPD does this represent?
7.w: Learning new software enhances skills.

n.3: Learning is the opposite of ignoring gaps.
n.2: Finance is not the focus here.
n.1: Risk avoidance is unrelated.
n.4: CPD is not just about compliance.

7.q: On a cross-functional project, a project manager reviews how the Organisation Breakdown Structure and Responsibility Assignment Matrix work together. Which TWO outcomes would demonstrate that the OBS and RAM have been effectively integrated?
7.w: OBS defines roles, RAM assigns them effectively.

7.q: A design decision on a new product must be settled in a meeting attended by both specialist engineers and non-technical business sponsors who need to understand the trade-offs. Which communication approach would be MOST effective for the project manager to use in this situation?
7.w: Verbal discussion supported by visuals bridges understanding gaps between audiences.

n.1: Specifications may overwhelm non-technical stakeholders.
n.0: Raw data lacks interpretation.
n.3: Links alone do not ensure understanding.
n.2: Formal reports may not facilitate interaction.

7.q: A project manager is developing an engagement strategy for a broad set of stakeholders at the start of a change programme and wants it built on the right foundations. Which TWO factors are most critical to take into account when developing the strategy?
o: Stakeholder influence and level of interest
7.w: Influence, interest, and expectations drive engagement strategies.

n.3: Formatting is not critical.
n.4: Location is not a primary factor.
n.0: Preferences should not drive strategy.

7.q: A significant change has been approved that alters aspects of the deliverable being produced on a construction project. Why should the project manager review the quality management plan following such a change?
o: To ensure deliverables continue to meet standards
To speed up delivery regardless of quality
7.w: Quality plans must reflect changes to maintain expected standards.

n.3: Documentation should be adequate.
n.4: Quality should not be sacrificed for speed.
n.0: Stakeholders remain important.
n.1: Closure occurs after delivery.

7.q: A project relies on an operational team whose routine work carries its own threats, such as system outages and seasonal workload spikes. How can risks in business-as-usual activities affect the schedule of a project?
o: By guaranteeing extra resources are assigned to the project
By causing delays to project tasks if BAU risks materialise
By transferring all BAU risks onto the project risk register
By automatically extending the project deadline to absorb them
By lowering the project's agreed quality requirements
7.w: BAU risks can disrupt project timelines if they materialise.

n.2: Scope changes are managed through formal change control, not BAU risks.
n.3: Contingency is needed precisely because risks exist.
n.4: Risks generally slow down progress, not speed it up.
n.0: Staff availability may decrease if BAU is affected.

7.q: A business case sets out the expected benefits and costs in careful detail, but makes no mention of the risks involved in delivering the work. What is the most likely consequence?
7.w: Ignoring risk can lead to unrealistic expectations of viability.

7.q: A sponsor regularly instructs individual team members on task priorities, bypassing the project manager. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Clearer accountability because team members receive senior direction
Better benefits realisation because decisions are made faster
Improved strategic alignment because the sponsor is closer to delivery
Undermined project manager authority and confused operational control
7.w: Sponsors should provide strategic direction and oversight, not bypass the project manager in operational task management.

8.q: A project team using Belbin's team roles is at risk of settling for a mediocre outcome and needs someone to push it harder and drive progress past the obstacles it faces. Which Belbin team role is typically responsible for challenging the team to improve and overcome these obstacles?
8.w: Shapers drive the team forward and push for improvement.

n.1: Teamworkers focus on harmony.
n.4: Resource Investigators bring in external opportunities.
n.0: Plants provide ideas.
n.2: Implementers turn plans into actions.

8.q: A team member is capable but is struggling with self-confidence and doubts their ability to take on new work. If the project manager adopts a coaching approach, how can it best help this individual?
o: By focusing only on technical training
By encouraging self-reflection and setting personal goals
By assigning more complex work immediately
8.w: Coaching supports confidence through guided reflection and achievable goals.

n.3: Increasing complexity too soon may undermine confidence further.
n.2: Ignoring the issue won't support the team member's growth.
n.0: Technical training is helpful, but coaching is more holistic.
n.4: Delegating all responsibilities may overwhelm the team member.

8.q: As part of solicitation, a procurement team approaches the market to gather background information and then invite formal proposals from potential suppliers for an upcoming package of work. Which two documents are typically issued to suppliers during this solicitation stage?
8.w: RFIs and RFPs are formal solicitations issued to gather information and proposals.

n.3: Purchase orders come after selection.
n.0: SLAs and contracts are post-award documents.
n.4: Change orders modify existing contracts.
n.2: Budgets and schedules are internal plans.

8.q: While conducting a business case review, a project manager is careful to respect governance and configuration management rules. In line with good practice, which of the following actions should NOT occur during a business case review?
o: Documenting the assessed impact of changes
Engaging affected stakeholders in the review
Changing the baseline without proper approval
8.w: Baselines require formal approval before any changes are made.

n.0: Impact documentation is standard practice.
n.3: Stakeholder engagement is critical.
n.2: Cost updates reflect current information.
n.1: Benefit revisions ensure accuracy.

8.q: While preparing deliverables, a project professional finds they are unsure whether their work meets a particular technical standard that applies to their field. Taking a professional approach, what is the best way for them to resolve this uncertainty?
o: Wait for someone else to notice
Make a guess and move forward
Consult the relevant professional body or standard-setting organisation
8.w: Professional bodies are the most authoritative source for technical standards.

n.3: Guesswork increases risk.
n.1: Popular opinion may be incorrect.
n.2: Waiting can cause non-compliance.
n.0: Each industry has specific standards.

8.q: During testing, heated debates among the team surfaced several critical flaws that would otherwise have been missed, but the arguments also pushed the delivery timeline back. Which pair of impacts does this represent?
8.w: Conflict improved quality detection but caused schedule delays.

n.1: Team cohesion and cost reduction aren’t the impacts described.
n.3: Morale and resource gain aren’t both described.
n.0: Governance and approval speed are unrelated.
n.2: Scope reduction and budget increase don’t match the scenario.

8.q: A project manager observes that a team is beset by ongoing disagreements, with members openly challenging one another and roles that remain unclear. Which stage of team development are they most likely experiencing?
8.w: The storming stage is marked by conflict and the clarification of roles.

n.4: Performing is characterised by high effectiveness, not conflict.
n.2: Norming comes after storming, with increased harmony.
n.0: Adjourning occurs at project close.
n.1: Forming is when the team is just coming together.

8.q: As a construction project progresses from its early feasibility work through to detailed design, the range around its cost and schedule estimates gradually becomes tighter, consistent with the estimating funnel. Which factor most directly drives this narrowing of the estimating funnel over time?
8.w: The funnel narrows as uncertainty reduces due to improved information and clarity.

8.q: While appraising the options for a proposed change to a product's specification, the project manager wants to understand how robust each option remains if the underlying estimates and assumptions turn out to be inaccurate. What is the purpose of carrying out sensitivity analysis in this situation?
o: To allocate the budget across the work packages
To identify and record all new project risks
To define team roles and responsibilities in full
To rank stakeholders by their level of influence
To understand how changes in assumptions affect outcomes
8.w: Sensitivity analysis evaluates how varying inputs influence results, supporting robust decisions.

n.3: It is not intended to cause delays.
n.1: Stakeholder roles are managed separately.
n.0: Risk registers are created independently.
n.2: Budget allocation is separate from sensitivity analysis.

8.q: A quality reviewer is examining several examples of project progress reporting in order to identify poor practice. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates ineffective progress reporting?
o: Reporting key milestones achieved and upcoming risks
Using visual indicators for status updates
Providing concise summaries tailored to stakeholders
Including both qualitative and quantitative data
8.w: Reporting deviations without impact lacks context and limits decision-making.

8.q: A project manager is initiating a project in a heavily regulated sector where breaches carry significant consequences. Being aware of the relevant legal and regulatory requirements is essential for what primary reason?
o: To ensure the project operates within the law and meets required standards
To reduce the amount of project documentation needed
To transfer all legal accountability onto the project sponsor
To limit the involvement of external regulatory bodies
To justify extending the project schedule and budget
8.w: Operating within the law is essential for project legitimacy and success.

n.2: Profit is not the only concern for managers.
n.4: Meetings are still necessary for coordination.
n.1: Delegation does not remove legal obligations.
n.3: Communication is vital for compliance.

8.q: A project must undergo frequent regulatory audits and comply with fixed reporting standards throughout delivery. Considering these constraints, which life cycle would be least appropriate for this project?
8.w: Agile may struggle to meet the documentation and structure needed for frequent audits.

n.2: Linear life cycles are audit-friendly due to documentation.
n.3: Hybrid models can incorporate necessary structure.
n.4: Stage-gated processes help manage compliance.
n.1: The V-model supports traceability and testing.

8.q: A project manager is choosing a delivery approach and observes that the way the organisation behaves is shaping the decision as much as the project itself. Which of the following scenarios best reflects cultural influence on life cycle selection?
o: Governance board approves all funding upfront
Client imposes penalties for late delivery
Project selected based on available budget
Organisation encourages experimentation and minimal hierarchy
8.w: Cultures that embrace experimentation and reduced hierarchy are well suited to iterative and Agile life cycles.

n.3: Budgeting is financial, not cultural.
n.1: Full funding up front suits linear planning.
n.2: Penalty clauses suggest rigid control.
n.0: Milestone payments reflect contract terms more than culture.

8.q: A project sponsor asks for a cost-benefit analysis before deciding on a change. At which stage in change control is this MOST likely to happen?
8.w: The detailed evaluation includes cost-benefit and impact analyses before recommendation.

n.1: Implementation follows evaluation and decision-making.
n.4: Initial evaluation is high-level, not in-depth.
n.2: Plans are updated only after approval.
n.0: Reviews happen after project completion, not during change control.

8.q: A project manager is establishing the quality standards that outputs on a project must meet and is asked to explain why defining these standards matters. In quality planning, what is the primary purpose of defining standards?
o: To ensure every stakeholder is satisfied straight away
To provide a basis for measuring and validating outputs
To reduce the amount of project documentation required
To eliminate all quality-related risks on the project
To cut project costs regardless of output quality
8.w: Standards provide the baseline against which outputs are measured and validated.

n.2: Documentation is not the primary purpose.
n.0: Satisfaction depends on meeting requirements.
n.3: Risks cannot be eliminated entirely.
n.4: Cost should not override quality standards.

8.q: During quality planning, a key stakeholder insists that the product must simply be 'user-friendly', without offering any further definition. The project manager needs to make this expectation manageable. How should this be handled in quality planning?
o: Reject the requirement as it cannot be measured
Convert the requirement into measurable usability criteria
Accept the subjective term without clarification
Assign responsibility to the design team only
Delay addressing it until user testing
8.w: Subjective expectations must be translated into measurable criteria to be managed effectively.

n.0: Rejecting ignores stakeholder needs.
n.2: Creates ambiguity.
n.4: Delays risk resolution.
n.3: Does not define measurable outcomes.

8.q: A stakeholder prefers to receive brief informal updates, but the project's governance requires structured formal reporting. What is the most appropriate adjustment for the project manager to make?
o: Adapt communication approach while maintaining control
8.w: Balancing stakeholder preference with governance ensures effective communication.

n.1: Rigid approaches reduce engagement.
n.0: Removing structure risks control.
n.4: Frequency is not the issue.
n.2: Ignoring preferences reduces alignment.

8.q: A project's completion date has slipped because newly introduced regulations require additional safety checks to be carried out before handover. This delay is best described as an example of which of the following?
o: Scope creep introduced by additional requirements
Ineffective risk response to a known threat
Poor initial estimation of the project timeline
Legal and regulatory impact on project schedule
Resource shortfall affecting planned project activities
8.w: New laws can alter timelines and project plans.

n.2: Team conflict is not the cause in this scenario.
n.0: Budget is not the issue here.
n.1: Stakeholder mapping is unrelated to safety checks.
n.4: Project methodology may need adapting, but is not the cause here.

8.q: A project is entering detailed planning, but key specialist resources are only partially available due to ongoing operational commitments. Which approach best supports effective resource allocation under these constraints?
o: Delay planning until all resources are fully available
Prioritise critical activities and assign scarce resources to them first
Evenly distribute limited resources across all tasks
Increase overall project duration to match resource availability
Allocate resources based on initial estimates and adjust later
8.w: Focusing scarce resources on critical activities ensures progress on tasks that directly impact project completion.

n.4: Reactive adjustment increases risk and inefficiency.
n.0: Waiting delays the project unnecessarily.
n.2: Spreading resources reduces effectiveness on key tasks.
n.3: Extending duration may not address priority constraints.

8.q: On a linear project, a change authority has considered the recommendation for a proposed change and reached its decision. Which activity typically follows the 'recommendation' stage in the change control process?
8.w: After a recommendation is made, relevant project plans are updated to reflect the decision.

n.4: A new business case is not always required after every recommendation.
n.0: Lessons learned are reviewed after implementation, not after recommendation.
n.3: Procurement cancellation is unrelated to most changes.
n.2: Team-building is not a change control activity.

8.q: A project team is debating whether to maintain a single coordinated plan or to let each function run its own separate documents. As project manager, you argue for an integrated approach. Why is integration important in a project management plan?
o: It enables each team member to plan and work in isolation
It ensures all elements of the project work together towards common objectives
It provides a guarantee that the project will encounter no risks
It replaces the requirement for a separate project business case
It removes the need to maintain any formal project documentation
8.w: Integration aligns objectives, controls and processes for project success.

n.0: Teamwork is essential.
n.4: Documentation is still required.
n.2: Risk cannot be eliminated.
n.3: Business cases are still needed.

8.q: A project team knows a risk is unlikely but chooses to do nothing until it happens. What response is this?
8.w: Acceptance is choosing to tolerate a risk, taking no action until it materialises.

n.2: Avoidance seeks to remove the risk proactively.
n.1: Transfer moves risk to another party.
n.4: Exploit is for opportunities.
n.0: Share is for opportunities.

8.q: A project manager observes that, working together, her team consistently achieves more than the sum of what its members could produce individually. Which concept does this best illustrate?
8.w: Synergy means the team's combined effort exceeds the sum of individual contributions.

n.2: Micro-management limits team effectiveness.
n.3: Effective teams avoid dominance by one person.
n.1: Coordination is high in effective teams.
n.4: Silo working is a barrier to teamwork.

8.q: A newly identified risk carries a proposed response whose cost exceeds the financial limits delegated to the project manager, so a higher authority must sign it off. What ensures the correct approval and escalation process is followed?
8.w: The governance framework defines who can approve what and the escalation path.

n.2: Stakeholder analysis is important, but governance sets approval limits.
n.3: Brainstorming does not define authority.
n.1: Communication plans support, but do not define, authority.
n.4: Procurement strategy relates to suppliers, not escalation.

8.q: After initial briefings, stakeholders still have unrealistic demands. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of actively managing stakeholder expectations?
o: Greater trust in the project team
8.w: While expectation management reduces scope changes, it cannot eliminate them completely—some changes are inevitable.

n.2: Engagement improves when expectations are managed clearly.
n.0: Clear expectations help to mitigate and reduce conflicts.
n.3: Trust grows when stakeholders feel heard and understood.
n.4: Quick decision-making is enabled by clear, shared understanding.

8.q: At the outset of planning a delivery project, a project manager works to surface limitations on resources, funding and time as early as possible. In resource planning, what is the main purpose of identifying constraints early?
o: To enable realistic scheduling and decision-making
8.w: Constraints inform feasible plans and trade-offs.

n.1: Not the primary purpose.
n.4: Indirect outcome.
n.3: Reporting is secondary.
n.0: Documentation is not the focus.

8.q: A project manager is determined that the solution developed will be as close to optimal as possible for the organisation. Which combination of actions should they prioritise?
o: Rely solely on the original requirements list throughout
Evaluate requirements for value, prioritise delivery, and incorporate feedback iteratively
Let the team self-organise without any stakeholder input
Complete all technical tasks first and weigh value later
Deliver every requested feature regardless of its value
8.w: An optimal solution is built by evaluating, prioritising and adapting based on feedback.

n.0: Requirements can change as more is learned.
n.4: Value analysis prevents waste.
n.3: Value should inform all technical decisions.
n.2: Leadership and input improve outcomes.

8.q: While preparing the quality management plan, a project manager is asked by the sponsor to relate each proposed quality indicator back to the objectives set out in the business case. In quality planning, why is it important to link quality indicators to business case objectives?
o: To provide evidence that the project is delivering expected benefits
To remove the need for separate quality control activities entirely
To transfer accountability for quality onto the project sponsor
To guarantee that the project produces a completely defect-free output
To reduce the number of quality reports the team must produce
8.w: Linking indicators to business case objectives demonstrates delivery of value.

n.2: Stakeholder involvement is still necessary.
n.3: Zero defects is an aspiration, not a guarantee.
n.4: Reports should meet, not avoid, requirements.
n.1: All planning processes are important.

8.q: A project manager reviews a newly submitted change request but is not yet confident about its full effect on the project's cost, schedule and objectives. Which of the following is an appropriate reason to defer the change?
o: Project is behind schedule and needs speeding up
Lack of sufficient data to assess impact
All required resources are available now
8.w: Deferring allows time to gather more information for a sound decision.

n.1: Consensus suggests proceeding, not deferring.
n.4: Urgency calls for immediate action.
n.0: Speeding up needs prioritizing changes, not deferring.
n.3: Availability of resources supports proceeding.

8.q: Midway through delivery, a new standard governing sustainability in projects is published and applies to work of the kind the team is undertaking. Acting professionally, what is the project manager's responsibility in this situation?
o: Apply the standard only to future projects, not current ones
Wait for the standard to become legally mandatory first
Ensure the project complies with the new standard
Adopt the standard only if it reduces project costs
Delegate compliance for the standard entirely to the sustainability team
8.w: Managers must keep up to date and comply with new standards.

n.0: Previous standards may be out of date.
n.4: Proactive compliance prevents problems.
n.3: Informal contacts are not sufficient.
n.1: Ignoring guidance is non-compliant.

9.q: A project manager is working to secure genuine stakeholder agreement to a transition plan before go-live. A colleague lists several things she considers essential to doing this well, but one of them would actually damage the consensus being sought. Which is NOT essential when gaining stakeholder agreement on a transition plan?
9.w: Ignoring minority concerns risks gaps in the plan and undermines true consensus.

n.3: Clear role documentation prevents confusion.
n.1: Impact assessments show how changes affect stakeholders.
n.0: Joint reviews build shared understanding of risks.
n.4: Formal sign-off confirms commitment and accountability.

9.q: A project team is selecting measures that will let them monitor whether their outputs are meeting the agreed standards. In this context, what is a quality indicator?
o: A summary of the resources allocated to quality activities
A measurable attribute used to assess whether outputs meet defined standards
A checklist of the tasks required to build a deliverable
A record of all defects found during product testing
A statement of the project's overall quality objectives
9.w: Quality indicators are metrics that assess conformity to standards.

n.2: Deliverables lists show outputs, not indicators.
n.3: Meeting frequency does not measure quality.
n.4: Profit is a financial, not a quality, measure.
n.0: Risk breakdowns are unrelated.

9.q: A public-sector organisation requires full documentation and audit trails, while also seeking flexibility in delivery. What approach is most suitable?
9.w: Hybrid life cycles balance the need for control and flexibility, ideal for structured yet adaptive delivery.

n.4: Iterative lacks formality in documentation.
n.0: Agile delivery may not support strong governance.
n.3: Linear lacks flexibility in delivery.
n.1: Incremental is focused on delivery stages, not governance adaptation.

9.q: A project operating in a heavily regulated sector must keep track of every policy, standard and statute it has to comply with. The project manager needs the governance tool that captures these obligations. Which governance tool lists applicable policies and regulations for a project?
9.w: A policies and regulations register captures all relevant rules that must be complied with during the project.

n.0: A risk register logs project risks, not policy requirements.
n.3: A communication plan defines information flow, not regulations.
n.2: A stakeholder map identifies stakeholders, not policy details.
n.1: An issue log records problems, not governance policies.

9.q: A sponsor is explaining to a sceptical department head why the effort of maintaining clear governance procedures is worthwhile for their project. One claimed advantage, however, is not something governance actually provides. Which is NOT a benefit of having clear governance procedures?
9.w: Governance sets limits; it does not grant unlimited spending power.

n.0: Transparency is a key governance outcome.
n.1: Procedures help avoid repeated work.
n.2: Stakeholders trust clear governance.
n.3: Consistency in decisions comes from defined procedures.

9.q: A project manager is drawing up a shortlist of quality indicators for a new product-development project and wants to be sure the chosen measures will genuinely reflect performance. When deciding which indicators to adopt, what should be considered?
o: How well they measure desired outputs and support business benefits
How easily they can be collected without adding project cost
How many indicators the assurance team is able to review
Whether industry competitors are currently tracking the same measures
Which measures the project sponsor personally prefers to see
9.w: Indicators should relate directly to output quality and benefit delivery.

n.1: Personal favourites may not add value.
n.3: Competitors' metrics may be irrelevant.
n.2: Office colour is not related to quality.
n.4: Meeting numbers do not measure output quality.

9.q: As a project approaches handover, the customer is invited to trial the completed deliverables against their stated requirements before formally receiving them. What is the benefit of using acceptance testing as a quality control technique?
o: It ensures all outputs are produced at the lowest cost
It speeds up project closure regardless of results
It confirms that deliverables meet agreed success criteria before handover
It removes the need for quality planning
It replaces the need for user feedback
9.w: Acceptance testing confirms deliverables meet user-defined success standards.

n.1: Closure should follow full acceptance.
n.4: Feedback is still valuable.
n.0: Cost control is not the main aim.
n.3: Planning is always required.

9.q: An organisation delivering a major capital project wants a single, regularly updated document in which threats to the project's finances can be recorded, monitored and reviewed over time. Which report is most appropriate for monitoring ongoing financial risks?
9.w: The risk register is used to track all project risks, including those affecting finance.

n.4: Procurement registers are for purchases.
n.1: Resource sheets are not used for risk tracking.
n.3: Stage plans are schedules, not risk tools.
n.2: Issue logs track problems but not proactively like a risk register.

9.q: Stakeholders on a programme have differing needs: some want to check live progress at any time, while others require formal periodic summaries. Which combination offers both real-time data visibility and structured formal updates?
o: Ad hoc hallway conversations and rumor control sessions
Unplanned social gatherings and mass texting
Video game simulations and comic strips
Interactive project dashboard and scheduled status reports
9.w: Dashboards provide live data; status reports deliver formal, periodic summaries.

n.0: Hallway chats and rumor control aren’t reliable formal channels.
n.2: Simulations and comics are irrelevant to formal project updates.
n.1: Social gatherings and mass texts lack structure and consistency.
n.4: Flyers and pigeons are outdated and not timely or formal.

9.q: During supplier selection for a technically demanding project, an evaluation panel is tempted to choose the bidder with the strongest technical solution and give little weight to other factors. What is the key risk of selecting suppliers based solely on technical capability?
9.w: Ignoring cost can make the project commercially unviable.

n.4: Capability improves quality.
n.3: Not directly related.
n.2: Decisions are not necessarily simpler.
n.0: Scope is unaffected.

9.q: A project manager who consistently demonstrates strong emotional intelligence has led several teams over recent years. What is a common outcome typically seen among the teams that such a leader manages?
o: A focus only on individual achievement
9.w: EI builds trust and improves team cooperation.

n.4: EI promotes collaboration over competition.
n.3: Feedback is important in any leadership style.
n.1: Some conflict is inevitable; EI helps manage it.
n.0: Staff turnover can still occur.

9.q: A project team delivers functionality in small increments, refining requirements after each release based on stakeholder input. Which characteristic of an iterative life cycle is being demonstrated?
o: Completion of all design before build begins
Incremental delivery supported by feedback loops
9.w: Iterative life cycles deliver in increments and use feedback to refine outputs.

n.1: Scope evolves in iterative approaches.
n.2: Sequential phases are linear.
n.4: Stakeholder involvement is typically high.
n.0: This reflects a linear approach.

9.q: A project manager is categorising expenditure and wants to identify a cost that changes in proportion to the amount of work carried out during delivery. Which of the following is most likely to be considered a variable cost in the project?
o: Monthly insurance premiums paid at a set fixed rate
Annual office lease payments fixed by the contract
Printing costs that increase with the number of reports produced
One-off fees paid for the initial project planning
The fixed salary of the permanent project manager
9.w: Variable costs change with the volume of activity, like printing.

n.0: Insurance is usually fixed over time.
n.1: Leases are typically fixed.
n.4: Permanent salaries are often fixed.
n.3: Planning fees are not volume dependent.

9.q: As a project approaches completion, the project manager needs a single reference that sets out how the finished deliverables will be moved from the project into live operational use, with the tasks, roles and timing captured in one place. Which document outlines the strategy for moving deliverables into operations?
9.w: The transition plan details tasks, roles, and schedules needed for a smooth operational handover.

n.4: A quality plan covers standards, not handover tasks.
n.1: A risk register tracks threats, not the overall transition strategy.
n.2: Procurement strategy relates to buying goods/services.
n.0: Communications plan focuses on stakeholder messaging, not full transition sequencing.

9.q: A project manager needs immediate confirmation that a safety-critical change has been understood by all site teams working remotely. Which communication method is most appropriate?
9.w: A direct verbal method with confirmation ensures both speed and understanding in a critical situation.

n.4: Email lacks immediate confirmation of understanding.
n.2: Passive updates may not be seen in time.
n.0: Weekly notes are too delayed.
n.1: Formal reports are too slow for urgent communication.

9.q: A software development project using an iterative approach needs test resources for every cycle. What does this illustrate about resource allocation?
o: Certain resources must be available repeatedly, not just once
Material resources are not used in software projects
Financial resources are always more important
Resource allocation is not required in iterative projects
Resources are only needed at the end
9.w: Iterative cycles require certain resources to be scheduled for multiple rounds.

n.4: Some resources are needed throughout, not just at the end.
n.2: Financial and non-financial resources may be equally critical.
n.1: Material resources (like hardware) can be necessary.
n.3: Resource allocation is required in every life cycle.

9.q: A project team is evaluating several proposed options and wants a member who can objectively analyse the ideas and weigh up their merits to help the team avoid costly mistakes. Using Belbin's model, which team role is best suited to this?
9.w: Monitor Evaluators critically assess ideas and help teams avoid errors.

n.4: Resource Investigators bring in contacts.
n.2: Shapers drive performance.
n.3: Teamworkers maintain harmony.
n.0: Specialists offer deep knowledge.

9.q: During the planning phase of a facilities upgrade, the project manager is preparing the quality plan and is deciding how much to consult users, sponsors and operational teams before setting the standards for the outputs. What is the BEST reason to involve stakeholders in quality planning?
o: To ensure the quality standards meet user expectations and business needs
To avoid having to document the project requirements
To reduce the overall cost of the project delivery
To remove the need for any product testing
To let only the project manager approve the standards
9.w: Stakeholder input ensures quality standards are relevant and accepted.

n.2: Cost may be affected, but is not the reason for involvement.
n.1: Requirements documentation is essential.
n.3: Testing is still needed.
n.4: Approval should not rest with one person.

9.q: A procurement lead is deciding which solicitation document to issue for a purchase whose specifications, quantities and standards are already fixed and unambiguous. The request for quotation (RFQ) is used when requirements are ______.
9.w: RFQs are issued when scope and specifications are clearly defined.

n.1: Ambiguous requirements need an RFI first.
n.3: Flexible requirements suit an RFP, not RFQ.
n.2: Changing requirements need further planning.
n.0: Subjective criteria require proposal evaluation, not fixed quotes.

9.q: A project manager wants to improve motivation after several team members say their work feels disconnected from the overall project purpose. Which response is MOST appropriate?
o: Reduce stakeholder contact so the team can focus on assigned tasks
Explain how their deliverables contribute to outcomes and stakeholder value
Increase reporting frequency so team members remain visibly accountable
Offer informal praise without changing how work is framed
Reallocate work randomly to create variety and reduce boredom
9.w: Connecting work to purpose and outcomes can improve intrinsic motivation by helping team members understand the value of their contribution.

n.2: More reporting may increase control but does not address lack of purpose.
n.3: Praise alone may help morale briefly but does not connect work to meaning.
n.0: Reducing stakeholder contact may further weaken understanding of project value.
n.4: Random reallocation may create disruption and does not address purpose.

9.q: A project team begins to openly challenge decisions, question authority, and experience interpersonal conflict as individuals assert their viewpoints. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: The team is regressing due to ineffective leadership and requires restructuring
The team is adjourning and disengaging from project objectives
The team has reached performing and is optimising its decision-making approach
The team is norming, as members establish stable working relationships
The team is in storming, where conflict is a natural part of development
9.w: Storming involves conflict and challenges as individuals assert themselves and roles are negotiated.

n.0: Conflict does not necessarily indicate regression; it is a natural stage.
n.2: Performing reflects stability and effectiveness, not conflict.
n.3: Norming involves reduced conflict and increased cohesion.
n.1: Adjourning is related to project closure, not active conflict.

9.q: A team member who was previously reliable begins underperforming after being assigned unfamiliar tasks. Which leadership response BEST reflects situational leadership?
o: Escalate the performance issue to senior management immediately
Shift to a more directive and coaching approach to support capability development
Remove the individual from the task to maintain overall team performance
Maintain the same level of delegation to reinforce expectations of independence
Ignore the issue to avoid damaging morale
9.w: Reduced competence in a new context requires more guidance and coaching to rebuild performance.

n.3: Maintaining delegation ignores the change in capability requirements.
n.2: Removing the individual prevents learning and development.
n.0: Immediate escalation bypasses appropriate leadership intervention.
n.4: Ignoring the issue risks further decline in performance.

9.q: During a mid-project audit, the assurance team discovers that documentation lacks traceability. What should be the next priority for assurance activities?
9.w: Strengthening documentation control restores traceability and ensures future compliance can be verified.

n.4: Reducing audits would risk further non-compliance going undetected.
n.1: More meetings do not directly fix traceability issues.
n.0: Outsourcing may help, but first internal controls should be enhanced.
n.3: Freezing change requests doesn’t address documentation gaps.

9.q: To keep a hybrid team connected, a leader introduces regular virtual check-ins and moves the team onto shared collaborative platforms for its day-to-day work. Reviewing the impact after several weeks, the leader assesses the effect on the team. What is the likely result?
9.w: Regular check-ins and shared tools keep all team members connected and engaged.

n.0: Role clarity improves with communication.
n.1: Engagement typically rises with inclusion.
n.2: Hybrid leadership should include all staff.
n.4: Sharing of ideas should increase.

9.q: A stakeholder claims they were not informed of a key decision, despite updates being shared via a collaboration platform. What is the most likely issue?
o: The decision was not documented formally
The platform was inappropriate for critical decisions
9.w: Critical decisions require more controlled communication methods than passive digital updates.

n.4: Clarity may be an issue but does not explain visibility failure.
n.3: Digital channels do not guarantee engagement.
n.1: Responsibility alone does not ensure communication effectiveness.
n.0: Documentation alone does not ensure awareness.

9.q: On a programme delivered across several business units, the Organisation Breakdown Structure has been developed separately from the Work Breakdown Structure, without cross-referencing the two. What risk does developing the OBS independently in this way create?
o: Loss of traceability between costs and deliverables
Misalignment between roles and work packages
Weaker definition of quality acceptance criteria
9.w: OBS must align with WBS to ensure responsibilities match work.

9.q: A project manager is explaining to a new team member how scope is handled in an iterative life cycle, where the complete solution is not known at the outset. Which statement best describes evolving scope in an iterative life cycle?
o: Scope is irrelevant to project success
Scope is defined only at project closure
Scope must be fully defined before delivery begins
Scope is progressively refined through delivery and feedback
Scope is fixed to ensure control
9.w: Iterative life cycles refine scope over time.

n.2: This is linear.
n.4: Scope is flexible.
n.0: Scope remains critical.
n.1: Scope is defined throughout.

9.q: While preparing the business case for a new product line, an analyst separates the factors within the organisation's own control from those arising outside it. In a SWOT analysis, which of the following pair are the internal factors?
9.w: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal to the organization.

n.3: Opportunities and Threats are external factors.
n.0: Political and Economic are PESTLE categories, not SWOT.
n.1: Technological and Environmental are also external PESTLE factors.
n.2: Volatility and Uncertainty are VUCA elements, not SWOT.

9.q: A project clearly sets out the benefits it intends to deliver, but it never defines how each of those benefits will actually be measured. What is the key issue this creates?
o: The project will exceed its budget
The benefits may not be aligned with strategy
The benefits cannot be verified or tracked effectively
The team will not understand their roles
9.w: Measurement criteria are essential to confirm whether benefits have been achieved.

9.q: While reviewing the issue log for a long-running project, a project manager notices several very similar issues have been raised and resolved individually over recent weeks. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this pattern?
o: The recurring issues are routine and can be ignored
Each issue should simply be closed as quickly as possible
The issues are coincidental and should be handled individually
There may be an underlying root cause not being addressed
The project is performing efficiently despite the recurrences
9.w: Recurring issues indicate systemic problems requiring root cause analysis.

n.2: Patterns suggest linkage.
n.4: Performance is likely poor.
n.0: Ignoring worsens the problem.
n.1: Closure without resolution is ineffective.

10.q: Early in the procurement process, the project team drafts a document defining the deliverables, standards and requirements against which suppliers will later bid. During which procurement stage does drafting this Statement of Work occur?
10.w: Drafting the SOW is part of planning the solicitation requirements.

n.1: Evaluation happens after the SOW is complete.
n.2: Negotiation follows evaluation.
n.3: Award is post-negotiation.
n.4: Close-out finalizes contracts.

10.q: Updated cost forecasts now indicate that the project is heading for a 15% overrun against its approved budget. In line with good practice, what must the project team do in response to this projected overspend?
10.w: Projected overruns require a business case reassessment to guide decisions.

n.0: Reducing testing may introduce quality risks.
n.2: Deadline extensions need baseline analysis first.
n.4: Budget increases demand justification.
n.1: Contract terminations aren’t the first step.

10.q: A newly appointed project manager is clarifying with the sponsor when matters should be raised to the governance board rather than handled within the team. He wants to recognise the circumstances that ought to prompt escalation. Which TWO situations should normally trigger escalation within project governance?
o: A routine task completed by the team
A planned meeting taking place as scheduled
A forecast breach of agreed tolerance
A decision needed beyond the project manager's delegated authority
A minor update to a team checklist
10.w: Escalation is appropriate when tolerances are threatened or decisions exceed delegated authority.

10.q: At a stage gate review, a project's costs have clearly risen and its benefits have fallen, yet the project is allowed to continue exactly as before with no reassessment. What has failed here?
o: The accuracy of the original cost estimates
The use of the business case for decision-making
The frequency of stakeholder progress reporting
The initial approval of the project scope
The project manager's control of delivery tasks
10.w: Stage gates should use the business case to reassess viability and inform continuation decisions.

10.q: The deadlines for two critical tasks fall within the same short window, forcing the team to juggle both at once with too little time to do either properly. The conflict the team then experiences arises from:
10.w: Schedule overlap forces competition for limited time, causing conflict.

n.4: Stable requirements don’t create timing conflicts.
n.3: Standardized tools improve consistency.
n.1: Positive recognition improves morale.
n.2: Clear communication helps prevent conflict.

10.q: A project manager wants to illustrate to the sponsor two of the ways in which unmanaged conflict can harm a project and its team. Which of the following pairs illustrates two possible negative impacts of conflict?
o: Faster decision making and stronger relationships
Improved risk management and cost savings
10.w: Conflict can reduce trust and increase stress as negative impacts.

n.1: Those are positive impacts of conflict.
n.2: Stakeholder alignment and creativity are positive.
n.4: Risk management and cost savings are benefits, not negatives.
n.0: Faster decisions and strong relationships are positive.

10.q: On a large programme, stakeholders have agreed to receive performance reports every fortnight rather than every day or once a month. What is the main advantage of adopting this reporting frequency?
o: Guaranteeing stakeholders act on every update
Removing all reporting effort from the team
Eliminating the need to verify report data
Balancing timeliness with effort to maintain data quality
Providing continuous real-time visibility of progress
10.w: Fortnightly reports provide timely insights while allowing adequate time to collect and verify data.

n.4: Daily reports may be excessive and burdensome.
n.2: Frequent reporting should not produce outdated data.
n.0: Regular, timely reports build trust.
n.1: Accuracy is improved by balanced frequency.

10.q: A project manager is deciding in which circumstances stepping back and using the avoiding conflict-handling mode would be justified. Which of the following is NOT a scenario where the avoiding mode is appropriate?
10.w: Avoiding is inappropriate for critical safety decisions.

n.1: Avoiding works for minor tasks.
n.4: It helps when emotions are high.
n.2: It suits trivial issues.
n.3: Delay can help gain perspective.

10.q: A project has completed its definition phase and is seeking approval to begin execution. Before work starts, the project board convenes a decision gate. What key benefit does this decision gate provide before the project moves into execution?
10.w: Gates formally authorize the allocation of resources for the next phase.

n.4: Defects aren’t resolved automatically by gates.
n.1: Satisfaction must be managed continuously.
n.0: Unplanned changes still require approval.
n.2: Completion timing isn’t guaranteed by a gate.

10.q: A project is aligned with corporate strategy but fails due to lack of support from senior management. What aspect of project context was underestimated?
10.w: Internal influence, particularly leadership support, is critical.

n.2: External factors are not the issue.
n.1: Technical complexity is not mentioned.
n.3: Scheduling is not the root cause.
n.4: Suppliers are not involved.

10.q: A project delivering a product across three countries faces different legal obligations in each jurisdiction, and the sponsor is concerned about staying compliant everywhere. Which governance tool helps ensure compliance in this situation?
10.w: Policies and regulations within governance frameworks ensure legal compliance across jurisdictions.

n.1: Branding is marketing-focused, not compliance-driven.
n.2: Planning techniques do not ensure compliance on their own.
n.0: Agile charts track work, not regulations.
n.4: Interview schedules relate to HR, not governance.

10.q: A project manager wants a visual way to track the consistency of a repeated manufacturing output over time and to see quickly when results move outside acceptable limits. What is the purpose of quality control charts in project management?
o: To assign approved budgets across the individual project tasks
To record the agreed terms of external supplier contracts
To monitor performance trends and identify deviations from standards
To map stakeholder influence against their level of interest
To schedule planned resource holidays and periods of availability
10.w: Control charts track quality trends and highlight when results fall outside tolerance.

n.0: Budgets are not managed on control charts.
n.1: Contracts are managed elsewhere.
n.3: Stakeholder matrices are unrelated.
n.4: Holiday planning is not a project control.

10.q: A project manager notices that the team has matured to the point where it can resolve issues internally and make sound decisions with little or no need for the leader to step in. In Tuckman's model, at which stage does a team become capable of making decisions without leader intervention?
10.w: Teams in the performing stage work autonomously and resolve issues internally.

n.3: Forming teams need guidance.
n.4: Storming teams still have conflicts.
n.0: Norming teams are building towards autonomy.
n.1: Adjourning teams are winding down.

10.q: A project adopts a fast, high-volume digital channel that pushes updates to stakeholders very quickly, but stakeholders report that important items are getting lost and overlooked among the many messages. What is the KEY disadvantage of this method?
10.w: Fast digital communication can lead to excessive information that stakeholders ignore.

n.4: Speed is high, not low.
n.1: Documentation may still exist.
n.3: Reach is often broad.
n.2: Cost is not the main issue.

10.q: A project is being delivered in a jurisdiction whose regulatory regime has been settled and consistent for many years, with no sign of sudden change. Given this stability, which VUCA element is the team LEAST likely to need to treat as critical?
10.w: A stable environment means low Volatility.

n.4: Regulations can still be unpredictable—Uncertainty.
n.1: Regulations can be interdependent—Complexity.
n.3: Interpretation can remain unclear—Ambiguity.
n.2: Economic is a PESTLE category, not VUCA.

10.q: A project manager observes that, several weeks in, the team is still struggling to reach the performing stage of its development and remains stuck in earlier stages. Which of the following is most likely to be causing this delay in the team reaching peak performance?
o: Unresolved conflicts and lack of trust
10.w: Conflicts and mistrust can keep a team stuck in the earlier stages.

n.3: Organisational support usually helps teams develop.
n.2: Clear goals speed up development.
n.1: Complementary skills benefit teamwork.
n.0: Good communication helps teams progress.

10.q: When setting up governance for a multi-party project, the sponsor wants to make explicit who is permitted to take which decisions and at what level. What is the primary purpose of delegated responsibilities in governance?
o: To clarify who can make decisions
10.w: Delegated responsibilities specify who has authority to make which project decisions.

n.4: Task scheduling is part of planning, not the purpose of delegation.
n.1: Resource allocation is managed separately from delegation authority.
n.0: Budgets are financial controls, not directly defined by delegation.
n.3: Communication planning is distinct from delegation of decision rights.

10.q: During a project review, the sponsor challenges delivery decisions made by the project manager. What is the most appropriate interpretation of roles?
o: The project manager should escalate every delivery decision to the sponsor
The sponsor should direct day-to-day delivery while the manager reports
Both the sponsor and project manager hold identical delivery responsibilities
The sponsor provides oversight while the project manager manages execution
The delivery team should arbitrate disputes between sponsor and manager
10.w: Sponsors oversee and challenge, while project managers deliver.

10.q: A software development project receives multiple change requests each week. What is a key advantage of iterative life cycles when managing change control?
o: They use only annual change control reviews
They accommodate frequent changes without disrupting the project flow
They ignore change requests to maintain stability
They eliminate the need for change logs
They delay all changes until the end of the project
10.w: Iterative life cycles are flexible and can accommodate ongoing change without major disruption.

n.2: Ignoring change requests is not best practice.
n.0: Frequent reviews occur in iterative, not just annual.
n.4: Delaying all changes is not how iterative projects operate.
n.3: Change logs are still required for accountability.

10.q: A project manager developing a business case for a proposed IT investment decides to run a SWOT analysis before presenting options to the board. What is the primary purpose of carrying out a SWOT analysis at this stage?
o: To map stakeholder communication needs and reporting requirements
To identify internal strengths and weaknesses alongside external opportunities and threats
To design the project team structure and reporting lines
To forecast the financial returns and payback period over five years
To schedule the project milestones and key delivery deadlines
10.w: SWOT’s core purpose is to assess internal strengths/weaknesses and external opportunities/threats.

n.3: Financial forecasting is outside SWOT’s scope.
n.0: Stakeholder communications are not covered by SWOT.
n.4: Scheduling is part of project planning, not SWOT.
n.2: Team structure design is separate from SWOT analysis.

10.q: A project manager is reviewing what distinguishes a genuinely effective team from a group of individuals who simply happen to work in the same area. Which of the following is a key characteristic of an effective team?
10.w: Effective teams have clear, common goals that everyone understands and works towards.

n.2: Overly strict hierarchy can stifle communication and flexibility.
n.1: Effective teams collaborate rather than compete internally.
n.0: Open communication is a hallmark of effective teams.
n.3: Accountability is essential for team effectiveness.

10.q: A sponsor is reviewing the business case for a transformation programme and notes that a major financial benefit is not expected to be realised until roughly two years after the project itself has closed. For the governance of this initiative, what is the key implication of this timing?
o: The project manager remains accountable for two years
The project should be extended until benefits are realised
Benefits management must extend beyond project delivery
The team should remain assigned indefinitely
The project is no longer viable
10.w: Benefits often extend beyond the project lifecycle and require ongoing management.

10.q: A project scope statement sets out the deliverables in considerable detail, but says nothing about what falls outside the project's boundaries. As delivery proceeds, what risk does this omission most directly create?
o: Scope creep due to undefined boundaries
10.w: Without defined exclusions, stakeholders may assume additional work is included, leading to scope creep.

10.q: During a review, a project professional receives constructive criticism about the way they have been engaging stakeholders on their current project. Acting professionally, what should they do in response to this feedback?
o: Reflect and seek training to improve
Defend their current approach without review
10.w: Responding to feedback with action leads to professional growth.

n.2: Ignoring feedback limits growth.
n.4: Openness to change is a strength.
n.0: Responsibility for development is individual.
n.3: Development is always ongoing.

10.q: A project team receives conflicting requests from different stakeholders. What is the best way to resolve this when prioritising requirements?
o: Defer the decision to the end of the project
Let the development team decide without consulting stakeholders
Implement both requests regardless of impact
Choose whichever is easiest to deliver
Facilitate a discussion to align priorities with business objectives
10.w: Stakeholder alignment and business objectives should guide requirement prioritisation.

n.2: Not all requests can or should be implemented.
n.3: Ease of delivery is less important than value.
n.0: Delaying can create project risk.
n.1: Stakeholder consultation is essential.

10.q: During a heated design discussion, the team's clashing viewpoints ultimately produced an inventive solution to the problem that none of them had considered on their own. Which impact of conflict does this best illustrate?
10.w: Debating different views stimulates enhanced creativity as a positive conflict impact.

n.2: Scope creep is a negative outcome of uncontrolled changes.
n.3: Resource depletion is a result of poor planning, not conflict-driven creativity.
n.4: Schedule slippage is a negative consequence, not this scenario.
n.0: Stakeholder confusion is not illustrated here.

10.q: While planning an upcoming phase, a project professional realises they lack knowledge in an area that will soon be important to their work. Taking a professional and proactive approach, what is their most appropriate action?
o: Seek learning opportunities to address the gap
Ask a colleague to do the work instead
Ignore the gap if it does not impact current tasks
10.w: Actively seeking learning closes gaps and supports professional growth.

n.2: Management may not be aware of every gap.
n.3: Gaps can affect future work.
n.1: Delegation does not develop personal skills.
n.4: Proactive action is more effective.

10.q: A project professional working in the UK must ensure their project complies with the requirements of GDPR when processing personal data. Which source is best for authoritative advice on meeting these obligations?
10.w: ICO is the UK's regulatory authority for data protection and GDPR.

n.4: Forums are not official sources.
n.1: Gossip is not reliable.
n.0: Business news is not authoritative for GDPR compliance.
n.2: Blogs may not be accurate.

10.q: A project team includes members from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences. What is a key benefit of this diversity?
o: It guarantees all team members will agree
It increases the potential for innovative solutions
It reduces the need for project management
It ensures every decision is made quickly
10.w: A diverse team brings varied perspectives, leading to greater innovation.

n.1: Agreement is not guaranteed by diversity.
n.4: Diversity may require more time for decision-making.
n.0: Conflict can still occur, even in diverse teams.
n.3: Project management remains essential regardless of diversity.

10.q: A project manager insists on completing all design work before any build activity begins. What principle of a linear life cycle is being applied?
10.w: Linear life cycles require phases to be completed before moving forward.

n.0: This contradicts linear sequencing.
n.3: This relates to iterative approaches.
n.2: Refinement is iterative.
n.4: Adaptive planning is not linear.

11.q: A project manager is weighing the trade-offs of using the collaborating conflict-handling mode to resolve a significant dispute. Which of the following is NOT a drawback of the collaborating mode?
11.w: High cooperativeness is a feature, not a drawback of collaborating.

n.4: Collaborating can indeed be time-consuming.
n.1: It requires mutual trust.
n.3: It demands open communication.
n.0: It needs willingness to share.

11.q: A project sponsor questions why the project manager is investing effort in identifying and managing uncertainty on a new product launch. What is a primary benefit of effective risk management in projects?
o: It reduces the need for stakeholder engagement
It increases the likelihood of project success
It shortens the project duration automatically
It guarantees zero issues will occur
11.w: Effective risk management makes project success more likely by anticipating and managing uncertainties.

n.4: Issues may still arise, even with good risk management.
n.1: Risks can be reduced or managed, not eliminated entirely.
n.0: Stakeholder engagement is always important, regardless of risk management.
n.3: Risk management does not directly shorten duration.

11.q: A project manager records a new risk but fails to analyse its potential impact. What is the main problem with this?
o: The team cannot prioritise or respond effectively
11.w: Without analysis, the risk cannot be properly managed or prioritised.

n.0: Not all risks need escalation.
n.1: Risks are only closed after resolution.
n.4: Only realised risks become issues.
n.3: The project plan may still be valid.

11.q: A project engages a supplier for support services whose volume will vary over time, and the buyer wants to be billed according to the hours and resources actually used. Which reimbursement method is most suitable for scalable services billed by usage?
11.w: Time-and-materials allows billing based on hours or units of service used.

n.2: Fixed-price is a total sum, not usage-based.
n.4: Cost-plus is cost reimbursement, not usage billing.
n.1: Target cost sets a baseline, not usage billing.
n.0: Per-unit is for discrete physical units, not service hours.

11.q: On a troubled project, no one is clear who approves risk responses, escalation paths are undefined, and the risk register is rarely reviewed by any oversight body. What is the likely result of such poor governance in risk and issue management?
o: Unclear decision-making and increased project risk
11.w: Without clear governance, risks and issues may be missed or mismanaged, increasing uncertainty.

n.1: Poor governance often leads to delays, not speed.
n.0: It increases, not guarantees, project failure risk.
n.3: Issues will still occur and may be ignored.
n.4: Poor governance can reduce morale due to confusion.

11.q: During planning for a product launch, a project manager deliberately structures the Cost Breakdown Structure so that it mirrors the Work Breakdown Structure. What is the primary benefit of aligning the two structures in this way?
o: Faster execution of the project activities
Clear linkage between costs and deliverables
Reduced overall stakeholder involvement in reporting
Simplified management of the project risks
Improved accuracy of the project schedule
11.w: Aligning CBS with WBS ensures costs are traceable to deliverables.

11.q: Following a scheduled project review that has produced new information, the project manager is considering whether to revise the plan. What is a common reason to re-plan activities after a review?
11.w: Re-planning incorporates new risk information to keep the plan realistic and achievable.

n.3: Celebrations don’t drive plan changes.
n.0: Communication reduction is unrelated to plan accuracy.
n.2: Close-down deliverables occur at project end, not during re-planning.
n.1: Team meetings aren’t eliminated by re-planning.

11.q: A project manager spends most of their time defending the business case to senior executives rather than managing delivery. What is the most likely role confusion?
o: The project manager is performing a sponsor-level responsibility
The project team has taken over governance accountability
The sponsor is too involved in operational delivery
The supplier is managing stakeholder expectations incorrectly
The project board has removed delivery authority
11.w: Defending business justification at senior level is primarily a sponsor responsibility, while the project manager manages delivery.

11.q: On a safety-critical project, the project manager must ensure that every stakeholder interprets risk information in the same consistent way. Which two data features ensure effective risk communication across the group?
o: Clarity in risk descriptions and standardized severity scales
Team holiday schedules and lunch orders
Office temperature logs and music playlists
11.w: Clear descriptions and standard scales ensure all stakeholders understand risk nature and magnitude.

n.2: Humor and color may distract from seriousness.
n.3: Financial/tax documents do not convey risk context.
n.1: Social details are irrelevant to risk communication.
n.4: Environmental logs/music are not risk metrics.

11.q: Partway through delivery, the sponsor calls a meeting to question whether the project should continue at all, given a significant shift in the organisation's business priorities. A stakeholder asks what role the sponsor is performing. What role are they fulfilling?
11.w: Sponsors ensure continued business justification.

11.q: While setting up the stakeholder register for an office relocation project, the project manager first wants to capture the most basic identifying details for every party involved before adding any engagement data. Which of the following should the register include?
11.w: A stakeholder register lists each stakeholder’s name and their role or position.

n.1: Budget and schedule are cost and time planning outputs.
n.3: Quality metrics belong to quality management.
n.0: Risk and issue logs are separate risk management registers.
n.4: Test cases are part of quality assurance.

11.q: During risk analysis, a project manager assesses a particular risk as unlikely to occur but judges that its impact would be severe if it did materialise. Given this combination of low likelihood and high impact, what is the best approach to managing it?
o: Monitor closely and have a contingency plan ready
Close the risk now because it is judged unlikely
Postpone any analysis of the risk until project end
Transfer the risk onto a different project altogether
