Take no action given its low likelihood of occurring
11.w: High-impact risks need to be monitored and contingency planned, regardless of likelihood.

n.4: Ignoring risks can lead to project failure.
n.1: Risks should only be closed when no longer relevant.
n.3: Risks should be managed in the current project.
n.2: Delays can increase exposure.

11.q: A project manager has produced a complete Product Breakdown Structure, but the Work Breakdown Structure derived from it does not consistently reflect the products it should deliver. Given the relationship between these two structures, what is the most likely issue?
o: The stakeholders were never properly aligned on the project objectives
The project schedule remained incomplete right through the planning stage
The required resources were all assigned before defining the work
The overall project scope was originally defined far too broadly
The transition from product structure to work structure is poorly managed
11.w: The WBS must logically derive from the PBS; inconsistency indicates poor translation from products to work.

11.q: Shortly before go-live, a transition readiness assessment finds that several key members of the support team do not yet have the system access they will need to keep the service running after handover. The project manager must decide what to do. What should be done?
o: Remove support staff from transition plan
Provision system access to support staff
11.w: Ensuring support staff have access is critical for post-go-live support and should be addressed immediately.

n.1: Indefinite delays are impractical; targeted fixes are preferable.
n.3: QA scope reduction risks undiscovered defects.
n.2: Removing staff undermines support readiness.
n.0: Change control maintains stability; it should not be disabled.

11.q: While defining the scope of a marketing project, the team is careful to separate the tangible things it will produce from the wider improvements the organisation hopes to gain. In the context of scope definition, what does the term 'output' refer to?
o: A tangible deliverable produced by the project
The summary of project lessons learned
A risk that could impact the project
A financial benefit realised by the organisation
11.w: An output is a tangible deliverable, such as a new product or report.

n.4: Benefits are achieved after outputs are realised.
n.2: Risks are managed separately and are not outputs.
n.1: Lessons learned are part of project closure, not outputs.
n.3: Stakeholder numbers do not define outputs.

11.q: On a delivery schedule, an activity that lies on the critical path is finished ahead of its planned finish date, and no other constraints currently limit the work that follows. The project manager is assessing what this means for the timeline. What is the most likely impact?
o: Other dependent activities will be delayed as a result
Float will increase evenly across all of the remaining activities
The critical path through the network will be eliminated
The project will automatically finish ahead of its deadline
The project end date may improve if no other constraints exist
11.w: Early completion of critical activities can reduce overall duration if no other constraints limit progress.

11.q: A project has repeatedly exceeded tolerance before issues are escalated. The project manager argues that escalation would slow delivery. What is the strongest governance concern?
o: Tolerances should be widened so that escalation is rarely required
The delivery team should decide when tolerances no longer apply
Escalation is being treated as optional rather than part of control
The sponsor should take direct control of all daily delivery risks
Decision authority should be delegated in full to the suppliers
11.w: Escalation protects governance control when tolerances are threatened or breached.

11.q: A consultant is advising several organisations on how best to structure their delivery approaches to match their working conditions. Which of the following scenarios would BEST justify the use of an iterative life cycle?
o: An infrastructure project with predefined specifications
A construction project with fixed milestones and output
A regulatory project with strict compliance deadlines
A procurement activity with set budget and scope
A marketing campaign where content is tested and refined weekly
11.w: Iterative life cycles are ideal for environments where continuous feedback and refinement are required, such as marketing campaigns.

n.1: Construction projects usually follow a linear life cycle.
n.0: Predefined scope suits linear delivery.
n.2: Compliance projects benefit from structure and predictability.
n.3: Fixed scope and budget align with linear approaches.

11.q: A project operating in a balanced matrix structure is facing delays. Team members are unsure which tasks to prioritise. What is the likely cause?
o: Insufficient stakeholder buy-in and engagement in the project
Conflicting direction from functional and project managers
Excessive reliance on rigid formal governance review processes
Inadequate project funding to complete the scheduled work
Absence of an approved and documented business case
11.w: In balanced matrix structures, dual authority can cause confusion over task prioritisation.

n.0: Stakeholder buy-in affects support, not task direction.
n.3: Funding issues are financial, not decision-based.
n.2: Governance processes help control, not cause confusion.
n.4: The business case justifies the project, not task assignment.

11.q: During a review meeting, the team notes that several deliverables do not align with the agreed standards. Assurance activities on the project aim to ensure ______.
11.w: Assurance checks that deliverables meet defined quality standards.

n.0: Cost is monitored under financial control, not primary assurance focus here.
n.3: Time relates to schedule control, not directly to this alignment.
n.4: Scope control manages requirements, not quality alignment specifically.
n.2: Risk management addresses potential issues, not deliverable quality.

11.q: A sponsor sets specific environmental, social and economic targets for a construction project and asks the project manager to establish ongoing sustainability monitoring. What is the primary purpose of this monitoring?
o: To track performance against environmental, social and economic targets
To boost team morale and stakeholder confidence levels
To reduce the volume of project reporting documentation
To justify increasing the overall project scope and budget
To provide grounds for extending the project deadlines
11.w: Monitoring ensures projects meet predefined sustainability targets across multiple dimensions.

n.3: Expanding scope is unrelated to monitoring sustainability.
n.1: Morale may benefit, but it is not the monitoring objective.
n.4: Deadlines are schedule concerns, not monitoring goals.
n.2: Documentation reduction conflicts with accurate monitoring.

11.q: A project sponsor wants to see how project costs are distributed across deliverables. Which tool should the project manager use to show this information?
11.w: The cost breakdown structure (CBS) allocates and visualises costs for each project deliverable.

n.4: PBS shows deliverables, not costs.
n.1: WBS focuses on work, not cost distribution.
n.0: Milestone charts show key events, not costs.
n.3: Network diagrams are used for scheduling, not cost allocation.

11.q: At the start of solution development, a project manager has gathered a long list of requirements from stakeholders. When evaluating these requirements, what should be done before assigning priorities to them?
o: Document each requirement in the technical specification
Begin building the highest-profile requirements immediately
Baseline the full requirements list for formal sign-off
Confirm the delivery order with the development team
Assess the feasibility and value of each requirement
11.w: Feasibility and value assessment is essential before prioritisation.

n.2: Testing follows design and build.
n.0: Scheduling comes after prioritisation.
n.3: Procurement is not the first step.
n.1: Project closure is the final phase.

11.q: A government agency must deliver a time-critical public safety system quickly and under formal oversight, yet the system will also need to evolve and adapt after it goes live. Which life cycle would most likely be used?
11.w: A hybrid approach provides initial structure and speed with future flexibility for evolution and change.

n.3: Linear lacks flexibility post-launch.
n.4: Pure Agile may lack enough structure for safety-critical work.
n.2: Waterfall is another name for linear and lacks adaptability.
n.1: Predictive is another term for traditional (linear) life cycles.

11.q: A change has been approved and the schedule revised, but the project manager does not pass the updated schedule on to the delivery team. What can failing to communicate the schedule updates cause on the project?
o: Conflicts in task execution and delays
Faster progress across the remaining tasks
Lower overall costs for the project
Reduced scope of the project deliverables
11.w: Lack of communication often leads to confusion and schedule conflicts.

n.1: Progress usually slows with confusion.
n.3: Satisfaction declines without clear updates.
n.2: Costs may increase due to inefficiencies.
n.4: Scope is determined by the change, not communication.

11.q: Having evaluated a proposed change, a project manager is deciding how to respond and lists the recognised courses of action open to them. Which of the following is NOT a typical option when assessing ways to address a proposed change?
o: Deferring the change to a later phase
Modifying the change to reduce impact
11.w: Ignoring a change is not a valid or responsible assessment option.

n.0: Accepting, modifying, rejecting, or deferring are valid options.

11.q: Before releasing funding for the delivery phase of a major infrastructure project, a sponsor insists on seeing a fully integrated project management plan. Why is it valuable for project sponsors to require an integrated project management plan before authorising delivery?
o: It confirms that the detailed technical design is fully complete before any planning begins
It replaces the need for holding regular stage-gate reviews throughout the delivery phase
It locks the project scope completely so that no further changes can ever occur
It gives assurance that all aspects of the project are coordinated and risks are managed
It transfers full accountability for all delivery outcomes onto the project manager alone
11.w: Sponsors want assurance the project is well planned, controlled and coordinated.

n.4: Progress should still be reviewed regularly.
n.0: Change is a normal part of projects.
n.1: The business case remains important.
n.2: Stakeholder input is vital throughout.

11.q: A project promising strong long-term benefits will require a large investment before any return is seen, and the board is weighing whether to commit the funds. What must the business case demonstrate?
o: That the project has minimal risk
That the team can deliver quickly
That the benefits outweigh the costs over time
11.w: Viability requires demonstrating that benefits justify the costs.

11.q: A project manager delivering a linear, phased project conducts a formal review of the risk register at every stage gate before authorising the next phase. Why is carrying out risk reviews at these points particularly important in a linear life cycle?
o: Linear projects rarely need any form of risk escalation
Formal risk reviews add value only at the point of closure
Iterative projects review their risks only at the final cycle
Stage gates provide natural points for formal risk review and control
Linear projects encounter far fewer risks than iterative ones do
11.w: Stage gates in linear projects are ideal for structured risk reviews and decisions.

n.4: Risks can change at any time in any project.
n.2: Iterative cycles also require risk reviews, but at different intervals.
n.1: Risk reviews should occur throughout the project.
n.0: Escalation may be required in any life cycle.

11.q: After initially plotting stakeholders on a power/interest grid, a project manager knows their positions should not be treated as fixed. Which TWO factors should trigger a reassessment of a stakeholder's position on the grid?
o: Standardisation of reporting templates and documentation approaches
Consistency of communication formats used across the project lifecycle
Changes in stakeholder influence due to organisational or project developments
Shifts in stakeholder interest resulting from project progress or outcomes
Personal preferences of the project manager regarding engagement style
11.w: Changes in influence and interest require reassessment.

n.1: Formats do not affect position.
n.0: Templates are not relevant.
n.4: Preferences are not valid factors.

12.q: A project team identifies a chance to adopt an innovative method that could deliver benefits, but decides not to pursue it because of the uncertainty involved. In choosing to forgo the opportunity, what is the key trade-off being made?
12.w: Choosing not to pursue an opportunity sacrifices potential benefits to reduce risk.

n.0: Not relevant.
n.3: Not the main trade-off.
n.4: Irrelevant.
n.1: Not applicable.

12.q: An organisation is weighing whether to move its delivery model so that dedicated teams are permanently assigned to individual projects. As it reviews the trade-offs, which of the following is a disadvantage of project-based structures?
o: Lack of role clarity for team members
Inefficient use of specialist resources across projects
12.w: Specialists may be isolated in project teams, making cross-project resource use less efficient.

n.0: Governance can be streamlined in project-based environments.
n.1: Decisions are typically fast due to direct control.
n.3: Reporting lines are usually clear under the project manager.
n.2: Roles are clearly defined in most project teams.

12.q: While building the schedule for a finance system upgrade, a project manager reviews the organisation's key operational reporting dates before fixing task timings. Why should a project manager assess business-as-usual deadlines when creating the project schedule?
o: To avoid conflicts that could delay project tasks
To set up more project meetings
To improve the company’s public image
To select a new project sponsor
12.w: Assessing BAU deadlines helps avoid clashes that can cause project delays.

n.2: More meetings do not solve scheduling conflicts.
n.4: Project sponsorship is unrelated to BAU deadlines.
n.1: Scope reduction is a separate decision.
n.3: Public image is not directly affected by BAU deadlines.

12.q: A retail chain rolls out a loyalty program. When planning benefits management, which document outlines roles and responsibilities for benefit delivery?
12.w: The benefits management plan defines roles and responsibilities for benefit delivery.

n.3: Register records benefits details but not roles/responsibilities.
n.1: Stakeholder engagement plan focuses on communication.
n.2: Resource plan covers resource allocation.
n.4: Risk plan covers risk handling.

12.q: A project team under time pressure decides to bypass configuration identification and move straight into producing deliverables. If configuration identification is skipped, what is the MOST likely risk?
o: Delayed sign-off of the project business case
Inaccurate forecasting of the remaining project budget
Higher procurement costs across the project supply chain
Uncontrolled changes and confusion about product versions
12.w: Without identification, changes can't be controlled and versions become unclear.

n.3: Delivery is more likely to be delayed by confusion.
n.0: Resource allocation may become harder.
n.1: Stakeholder numbers are unrelated.
n.2: Costs can rise due to rework and errors.

12.q: During a project, a change request is submitted to alter the design of a key deliverable. What is the immediate next step in the change control process after the request is received?
o: Initial evaluation of the change request
12.w: After a change request is submitted, the first step is to carry out an initial evaluation before any further actions.

n.3: Implementation only occurs after evaluations and approvals.
n.2: A detailed evaluation happens after the initial screening.
n.4: Plans are updated only after approval and decisions are made.
n.1: Stakeholder communication is important but not the immediate next step.

12.q: A motivated project team regularly takes the initiative and produces outputs quickly, but those outputs frequently fail to match what stakeholders were expecting. A governance review examines why this keeps happening. What is the most likely issue?
o: The team lacks the technical skills to deliver the outputs
Roles and responsibilities are unclear, particularly around direction and control
The governance framework imposes excessive review and control
The project manager is over-controlling routine delivery decisions
The sponsor is too heavily involved in day-to-day delivery
12.w: Misalignment often stems from unclear role boundaries and control mechanisms.

12.q: A project manager encourages small, incremental changes based on feedback rather than waiting for major redesigns. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: This approach increases risk due to frequent changes
This approach replaces formal governance processes
This approach supports continuous improvement through iterative adjustments
This approach reduces the need for stakeholder engagement
This approach is only suitable for linear projects
12.w: Continuous improvement often involves incremental adjustments based on feedback.

n.3: Stakeholder engagement remains important.
n.0: Incremental change can reduce risk.
n.1: Governance still applies.
n.4: It is suitable across different life cycles.

12.q: A project team needs to gather structured input from users and stakeholders to inform its requirements and decisions. Which two data collection techniques are commonly used in projects to obtain this information?
o: Magic eight balls and coin flips
12.w: Surveys and interviews gather structured insights from stakeholders and users.

n.3: Social events are not formal data techniques.
n.4: Psychic methods are not reliable data sources.
n.0: Random chance tools are not valid data techniques.
n.1: Informal social media content isn't structured data.

12.q: While creating a budget, a project team identifies several cost categories that overlap between work packages. What should they do?
o: Clarify and separate costs in the CBS to avoid double-counting
Transfer all the overlapping costs into the contingency reserve
Reassign the overlapping costs to individual stakeholders instead
Merge the overlapping costs into one line for simplicity

14.q: A project manager wants to introduce Agile delivery on a project and is assessing whether the surrounding culture will support that way of working. Which cultural trait would most likely support Agile delivery within the project?

n.4: Rigid processes contradict Agile values.

14.q: A project using an iterative life cycle wants to deliver a Minimum Marketable Product (MMP). What is the primary aim of this approach?

To build every planned feature before releasing to any customer
To reduce quality assurance so the product ships more quickly
To deliver enough value that the product can be sold to customers

14.q: A project manager is worried that the current plan will push several team members beyond their available hours, yet the contractual delivery date cannot be moved under any circumstances. Which technique is the most suitable for the project manager to apply in this situation?

More accurate and complete project documentation
Better stakeholder satisfaction with quicker delivery
Lower project risks through faster response

14.q: A risk response has been implemented but is not being monitored. What stage of the risk process is being neglected?

14.q: A project manager is drafting a high-level impact assessment for a proposed change and wants it to show how far the change would push back the project's key delivery points. Which of the following should this assessment include?

14.q: An assurance reviewer asks the project manager to explain what a verification audit achieves within configuration management. Which statement is TRUE about verification audits in configuration management?

14.q: A project is delivering a new IT system. Early workshops reveal conflicting stakeholder expectations about acceptable system performance levels. What is the MOST appropriate quality planning response?

Focus on meeting the highest expectation to avoid rework
Allow each stakeholder group to define their own performance benchmarks
Capture expectations as risks and manage them later
Define measurable acceptance criteria aligned to agreed standards

14.q: After a project has formally closed and been handed over to the business, the project manager decides to take on ongoing responsibility for realising its benefits. What is the main concern with this?

The team will not deliver outputs
The project will require less governance

14.q: A project team defines detailed technical standards but fails to engage end users during quality planning. What is the MOST likely consequence?

Improved compliance with relevant regulations and technical standards

Outputs that meet specifications but fail user needs

14.q: After smoothing a schedule, the project manager finds one specialist remains over-allocated during a critical activity. What does this most likely indicate?

The project manager should ignore the remaining overload
The activity should be removed from the critical path
Resource smoothing always requires extra budget
There is insufficient float to remove every resource conflict

14.q: Midway through a transformation project, market conditions shift and questions are raised about whether the investment is still worthwhile. The governance board looks to the sponsor for assurance. Which statement best reflects the sponsor's role in maintaining governance over project success?
